title: Build your site’s API
summary: From a button to a response: requests, keys, server routes and errors.

lessons.title: 1. Understand the journey
lessons.concept: An API receives a request and returns data.

explanation.text: The frontend is what you see. The backend checks requests and applies rules. An API is an entry point with an address, a method and a response format, often JSON. The database keeps information after the browser closes.

On L’ecomax: browser → /api/products?active=true → Supabase → JSON → product cards. GET reads, POST creates, PATCH updates and DELETE removes. Status 200 means success; 400 invalid input; 401 sign-in required; 403 access denied; 429 too many requests; 500 server failure.

exercise.task: Imagine opening a product list. Who requests the products? Who stores them?
hints: An API receives a request and returns data.
exercise.solution: The browser asks; the API route responds; Supabase stores the products.

summary: The browser asks; the API route responds; Supabase stores the products.

lessons.title: 2. Call your API from the site
lessons.concept: fetch requests data. You also need to check whether the request succeeded.

explanation.text: Read-only exercise: use this function in a test page in your local project. It requests three public products. await waits for the response; response.ok checks the status; json() turns the response into data. Also show loading, error and empty-list states in your component.

Open browser tools → Network. Inspect the URL, status and JSON. If the list is empty, check active products. Never return orders or customer data from a public API. Before a write, the server must verify the session, role, fields and limits.

exercise.task: On your local site, open /api/products?active=true&limit=3 in the browser.
hints: fetch requests data. You also need to check whether the request succeeded.
exercise.solution: You see JSON, not cards. The component turns that data into a display. An empty list can be valid.

lessons.title: 3. Create a route and connect a service
lessons.concept: The route.ts file defines the response at an API address.

explanation.text: In a test Next.js project, create app/api/hello/route.ts with this example, then open /api/hello. This file runs on the server. For an external API: read its docs, create a test key, put it in .env.local, then call its fixed HTTPS URL from this route using fetch. Use the authentication format required by the provider.

Keep private keys on the server: never NEXT_PUBLIC_, never GitHub, never screenshots. A Supabase publishable/anon key is intended for clients but needs suitable permissions and RLS. Secret/service_role keys bypass RLS: authorize every server operation. L’ecomax’s current variable names are in the file below; do not rename them without updating the code.

exercise.task: In your test project, create app/api/hello/route.ts, copy the example, run npm run dev and open /api/hello.
hints: The route.ts file defines the response at an API address.
exercise.solution: You should see message: Hello and ok: true. Replace Hello with Bonjour and reload to check your change.

lessons.title: 4. Reliability and debugging
lessons.concept: The HTTP status is a clue for finding an error.

explanation.text: On failure: 1) check URL and method; 2) inspect Network status; 3) read server logs without printing secrets; 4) check variables in the correct environment; 5) inspect database permissions. CORS concerns cross-origin calls: prefer your server route, do not disable browser security.

Add a timeout, pagination and rate limits. Do not blindly retry payments or order creation: use an idempotency key to avoid duplicates. For webhooks, verify the signature on the original body and record the event ID. For long tasks, use a job queue and worker instead of a request that waits indefinitely.

hints: The HTTP status is a clue for finding an error.
exercise.solution: 404 means not found. 200 means success. Note the address and status before investigating.
